note.question: How does the BOPS initiative affect store operations from an inventory perspective?
note.overview: Both traditional retailers and e-tailers have been implementing omnichannel strategies such as buy online, pick up at store (BOPS). We build a stylized model to investigate the impact of the BOPS initiative on store operations from an inventory perspective. The model considers two segments of customers, namely store-only customers who only make purchases offline and omni-customers who strategically choose between offline and online channels.

source.quote: We show that BOPS may either benefit or hurt the retailer depending on two fundamental system primitives: the store visiting cost and the online waiting cost.
We consider two segments of customers, namely store-only customers who only make purchases offline and omni-customers who strategically choose between offline and online channels.

(Our main results also hold when the inventory level in the DC is endogenized.) This assumption is reasonable when the retailer can make an emergency replenishment from another DC or a supplier with a relatively short lead time compared with that from the DC to customers.

On the one hand, customers can accurately value the ofﬂine product after inspection, and online customers without ﬁrsthand experience may risk having only partial knowledge on which to base their valuation.

We assume that omni-customers who eventually choose BOPS ﬁrst check online for the store inventory; if the store is out of stock, they then switch to the online channel with DC fulﬁllment if the utility of doing so is positive (see Gao and Su 2017a).
One of their main ﬁndings is that BOPS may beneﬁt or hurt the retailer, depending on the product characteristics.
